records.text: Chewy identifies several risks related to its dependence on suppliers. It depends on a number of suppliers and outsourcing partners—many located outside the U.S., particularly a significant portion in China for its private brand and non-consumable businesses—and disruptions to these relationships, whether from political and economic instability, labor problems, raw material availability, currency exchange rates, transport issues, tariffs, trade restrictions, or natural disasters, could materially and adversely affect its business [3]. The company also purchases significant amounts of products from suppliers with limited supply capabilities, and there is no assurance current suppliers can accommodate anticipated growth or continue supplying at preferential prices, with past disruptions already having occurred [14]. If significant pet product suppliers discontinue selling to Chewy or discontinue preferential pricing or exclusive incentives, this could negatively impact the business, and it can be challenging to persuade customers to switch pet food products, exacerbating the impact of losing a supplier [14]. Chewy also faces risk if it is unable to identify or enter into relationships with new suppliers to replace lost ones, potentially causing competitive disadvantage and business disruption [14][16]. Additionally, if premium pet food brands become more widely available through supermarkets, warehouse clubs, or mass merchants, or if suppliers offer preferential pricing/incentives to competitors, Chewy's competitive position and profitability could suffer, especially since certain suppliers currently provide trade allowances, cooperative advertising, and market development funds that could be reduced or discontinued [16]. Finally, Chewy notes broader supplier-related risks including product safety and quality control failures by suppliers (including private brand manufacturers) that could lead to recalls, litigation, or loss of consumer confidence [5].

NIKE also relies on 205 strategic Tier 2 suppliers for principal materials, with contract manufacturers themselves purchasing these materials [5].

Under Armour similarly outsources substantially all production to unaffiliated manufacturers, using 40 primary contract manufacturers across 17 countries for apparel and accessories in Fiscal 2026, with about 65% of production concentrated in Jordan, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Cambodia, and its top ten manufacturers producing approximately 69% of apparel/accessories output [12][14]. Footwear is even more concentrated, with substantially all production handled by just seven primary contract manufacturers, mainly in Vietnam and Indonesia [12][14].
